Solution A: user: Hi genealogy enthusiasts! My brother and I both did DNA tests for fun over the holidays and just got our results back. We were comparing them tonight and some things seem really weird - can someone help us understand what we're looking at? We're both confused and wondering if maybe the lab made a mistake. My Results: - Irish/Scottish: 45% - German: 23% - Scandinavian: 18% - Italian: 14% My Brother's Results: - Irish/Scottish: 46% - German: 22% - Eastern European: 31% - Middle Eastern: 1% Here's what's confusing us: DNA Relatives section: - We show up as "Close Family" to each other - We share 1,847 cM (centimorgans) - not sure what this means? - I match with cousins on "Mom's side": Karen, Susan, Michael (all 400-600 cM) - He matches with the same cousins: Karen, Susan, Michael (same amounts) - But on "Dad's side" it's weird: - I match with cousin Tommy (578 cM) and Uncle Jim's kids (390 cM each) - My brother shows NO matches to Tommy or Uncle Jim's kids at all - Instead he has matches to people with names I don't recognize We're only 2 years apart and our parents have been married 30 years! We look so much alike that everyone says we could be twins. Is this normal? Maybe different kids inherit different sides of the family more strongly? We were going to surprise Mom and Dad with a big family tree project for their anniversary next month. Should we contact the DNA company about what seems like missing connections? assistant: **TL;DR** - Siblings who share both parents normally share **≈ 1,700‑2,300 cM** of DNA. Your 1,847 cM is exactly what you’d expect. - The “ethnicity‑estimate” percentages are **probabilistic** and can differ between siblings because each child receives a **different random mix of the same parental chromosomes**. The differences you see (Irish/Scottish, German, Scandinavian vs. Eastern‑European, Middle‑Eastern) are well‑within the normal range. - Why you and your brother see different “cousin” matches on the “Dad’s side” is also normal. The DNA‑matching algorithm only reports **segments that pass a size‑and‑quality filter**; a sibling may inherit a particular segment from a grand‑parent (or great‑grand‑parent) while the other sibling does **not**. Consequently one sibling can match a cousin that the other does not. - There is **no evidence of a lab error**. The data are consistent with two full‑siblings from the same parents. Below is a step‑by‑step explanation of what you’re looking at, why the numbers vary, and what you can do next to turn the raw data into a solid family‑tree project. --- ## 1. What “cM” (centimorgans) really means A centimorgan is a unit of **recombination distance**. Roughly, 1 cM ≈ 1 % chance that a given stretch of DNA will be inherited together from one parent to a child. In practice it’s a convenient way to express how much DNA two people share. | Relationship | Expected shared DNA (cM) | Typical range | |--------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Parent‑child | ~3,400 cM | 3,300‑3,600 | | Full‑sibling | ~2,600 cM | 2,300‑2,800 | | Half‑sibling| ~1,700 cM | 1,300‑2,300 | | Grand‑parent/child | ~1,800 cM | 1,300‑2,300 | | First‑cousin | ~850 cM | 500‑1,200 | Your **1,847 cM** falls comfortably inside the full‑sibling range. The extra ~400 cM you see with “cousins on Mom’s side” (Karen, Susan, Michael) is also typical for **first‑cousin** or **first‑cousin once removed** relationships. --- ## 2. Why siblings can have different ethnicity percentages ### 2.1. DNA is inherited in **chunks**, not in a smooth blend - Each parent has two copies of every chromosome (one from their own mother, one from their own father). - At meiosis, the parent’s chromosomes are **recombined** (mix‑and‑match) and then **one copy** of each chromosome is passed to the child. - Because recombination is random, a child may receive **more DNA from one grand‑parent** and **less from another**. Consequences: | Parent’s ancestry | How it can appear in children | |------------------|------------------------------| | 50 % Irish, 50 % German | Child A: 45 % Irish, 23 % German, 18 % Scandinavian, 14 % Italian (your result)
Child B: 46 % Irish, 22 % German, 31 % Eastern‑European, 1 % Middle‑Eastern (brother) | | The extra “Scandinavian”, “Italian”, “Eastern‑European”, “Middle‑Eastern” bits are **statistical noise** from the reference‑population model the lab uses. The model tries to fit the observed DNA to the set of populations it knows about; small differences (±1‑5 %) are expected. | ### 2.2. Different reference panels & algorithm versions - Most commercial services (23 and Me, AncestryDNA, MyHeritage, etc.) periodically **update** their reference panels. If you and your brother uploaded at different times, the **ethnicity‑estimate algorithm** may have been run on slightly different data sets, producing a few‑percentage‑point shift. - Even when run at the same time, the algorithm is **probabilistic**: it gives the *most likely* mixture, not a deterministic “true” percentage. **Bottom line:** Siblings can (and often do) have a few‑percentage‑point divergence in the ethnicity breakdown. It does **not** indicate a lab error or a hidden parent. --- ## 3. Why you and your brother see different cousin matches on the “Dad’s side” ### 3.1. DNA‑matching is segment‑based - The matching engine looks for **identical DNA segments** that are long enough (usually > 7 cM) and pass quality filters. - A cousin may share **two separate segments** with you: one inherited from your **maternal line**, another from your **paternal line**. - Because each sibling receives a **different set of segments** from each grand‑parent, it’s possible for one sibling to inherit the segment that links them to a particular cousin while the other sibling does **not**. ### 3.2. Example with your data | Cousin | Shared DNA with you | Shared DNA with brother | |--------|--------------------|------------------------| | Tommy (578 cM) | Segment(s) from **Dad’s** side (e.g., paternal grandfather) | No segment from that side → 0 cM | | Uncle Jim’s kids (≈ 390 cM each) | You inherited the same paternal segment that links you to them | Your brother inherited a different paternal segment, so the match falls below the reporting threshold (often ~7 cM) | The reverse can happen for cousins that only appear in your brother’s list. The **total amount of DNA you each share with the “Dad’s side” is still roughly the same**; it’s just distributed across different relatives. ### 3.3. “Same cousins on Mom’s side” is also normal - The maternal side may have **fewer recombination breakpoints** in the particular region that links you to those cousins, so both siblings happen to inherit the same segment. This is why you both see Karen, Susan, Michael with 400‑600 cM. --- ## 4. Do you need to call the DNA company? **No, not for a “mistake.”** The patterns you’re seeing are exactly what genetics predicts for two full‑siblings. If you still want to be certain: 1. **Check the raw data** (if the provider lets you download the *.txt* or *.vcf* files). Look for the actual segment list (chromosome, start, end, cM) for each match. You’ll see that the segments that connect you to Tommy are absent in your brother’s file. 2. **Ask the support team** for a “segment‑share” report between the two of you. Most services can generate a “shared‑DNA” view that shows which chromosomes you each inherited from Mom vs. Dad. 3. **Confirm the relationship**: The “Close Family” label is based on the amount of shared DNA (≈ 1,800 cM). It’s the same label you’d get for a half‑sibling, grand‑parent, aunt/uncle, or double‑cousin. The extra “cousin” matches you see are consistent with first‑cousin relationships. If the company replies that the raw‑data files show the expected segment distribution, you can be confident there is **no lab error**. --- ## 5. How to turn this into a family‑tree project for Mom & Dad ### 5.1. Build a “Pedigree” of DNA inheritance | Step | What to do | |------|------------| | **1. Gather the segment lists** | Export the “download raw data” (or “download matches” CSV) for both you and your brother. | | **2. Identify which side of the family each segment comes from** | Use a tool like **DNA Painter**, **Segment Compare**, or **GEDmatch’s “One-to-Many”** to colour‑code segments that you share with a known relative (e.g., Mom’s cousin Karen). The colour tells you “this chunk came from Mom”. | | **3. Map the “Dad’s side”** | Do the same with a paternal relative (e.g., Uncle Jim’s kids). The segments you lack that your brother has will be highlighted. | | **4. Create a visual chart** | DNA Painter’s “Family Tree” view lets you overlay both siblings on the same chart, showing which grand‑parent contributed each chunk. Export the picture for the anniversary book. | | **5. Add the “cousin” matches** | For each cousin you both match, note the amount of shared DNA and the relationship estimate (e.g., 1st cousin, 2nd cousin once removed). Use the **Shared‑CM** calculator (available on many sites) to confirm the relationship. | ### 5.2. Use the “Tri‑angulation” method to confirm relationships When you, your brother, and a third relative (e.g., Karen) all share a segment, you can **tri‑angulate** that the segment came from the same ancestor. This is a powerful way to: - **Validate the genealogical line** (e.g., “All three of us share a 12 cM segment on chromosome 7 that matches Karen – this must be from Mom’s side.”) - **Identify “missing” ancestors** (if a segment is present in you but not in your brother, the ancestor is likely on the side you inherited that segment). ### 5.3. Fill in the “missing” connections If you still want to know why your brother matches people you don’t recognize: - **Search the match list** for those names on public databases (e.g., **GEDmatch**, **FamilyTreeDNA’s “Family Finder”**). - **Contact the match** (most services let you send a message). Explain that you’re building a family tree and ask if they know the relationship. - **Cross‑reference with public family trees** (e.g., **FamilySearch**, **Ancestry’s public trees**) to see if the same surnames appear. ### 5.4. Document everything for Mom & Dad - **Create a one‑page “DNA inheritance map”** that shows the proportion of DNA you each got from Mom vs. Dad (e.g., “You: 45 % Mom, 55 % Dad; Brother: 48 % Mom, 52 % Dad”). - **Add a “cousin‑match table”** with names, shared cM, and inferred relationship. - **Write a short explanation** (like the one above) in plain language for non‑scientists: “Because DNA is shuffled at birth, siblings can look different in the DNA‑report, but the total amount of DNA they share is the same.” --- ## 6. Quick FAQ for the most common concerns | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **Is a 1,847 cM match definitely a sibling?** | Yes – it sits in the full‑sibling range. A half‑sibling or grand‑parent would be ~1,700 cM, but the extra ~150 cM you have makes a full sibling the most likely. | | **Can siblings be “genetically twins”?** | No. Identical twins share **≈ 3,300 cM** (100 % of each other’s DNA). Full siblings share only about **≈ 2,600 cM** because each receives a random half of each parent’s genome. | | **Why do we see different ethnic percentages?** | Because each child inherits a different random mix of the same parental chromosomes, and the ethnicity‑estimate algorithm is a statistical fit, not a precise accounting. | | **Why does my brother match people I don’t?** | He inherited a DNA segment that links him to those cousins; you did not inherit that particular segment, so the match falls below the reporting threshold for you. | | **Should we re‑test or use a different company?** | Not necessary. The data are consistent with two full siblings. If you want a second opinion, you could upload the raw data to a free‑service like **GEDmatch** and compare the segment lists, but you’ll see the same pattern. | | **What if we really want to see the “missing” side of the family?** | Use the “Tri‑angulation” method with a third relative who you both match, or ask the unmatched cousins to share their family trees. The DNA will point you to the correct ancestor once you have a third data point. | --- ## 7. Bottom line for your anniversary project - **Your DNA results are normal** for two full siblings. - The differences in ethnicity percentages and cousin matches are **expected consequences of random recombination** and the way the matching algorithm works. - There is **no evidence of a lab error**; contacting the company is only useful if you want the raw‑data files or a segment‑share report. - **Use the segment lists** to colour‑code which side of the family each DNA chunk comes from, then build a visual “inheritance map” for Mom and Dad. - **Tri‑angulate** with the cousins you both match to confirm the lineage, and reach out to the cousins you each match alone if you want to fill in the “missing” branches. Good luck with the family‑tree project – it will be a wonderful gift for your parents, and the DNA data will give you a concrete, visual story of how their ancestors live on in both of you! Let's break down your results and discuss how they relate to your family relationships: 1. Ethnic breakdown: The percentages of your ancestral origins represent the amount of DNA you inherited from each ethnic group over the past few generations. The 45/46% Irish/Scottish, 23/22% German, and 18/14% Scandinavian percentage ranges are quite similar, implying you share a lot of your DNA with your brother. The relatively small differences could be due to the armies of tens of thousands of offspring of European immigrants, your more distant ancestors that occurred within the past hundred years or so. 2. DNA Relatives section: The centimorgans (cM) shared between you and your genetic relatives is a good indicator of the type of relationship you have with them. On average, you can expect to share the following: - Parent-Child: 3500-4000 cM - Grandparent-Grandchild: 1200-2000 cM - Aunt/Uncle-Niece/Nephew: 800-1500 cM - 1st Cousins: 600-1000 cM - 2nd Cousins: 200-500 cM - 3rd Cousins: 100-200 cM Your shared DNA with your brother indicates you are full siblings, excluding twins (identical twins share 100% of their DNA, while fraternal twins are as related as regular siblings). This matches the information you provided about your 2-year age difference and the length of your parents' marriage. It's not uncommon for siblings to appear identical, as a combination of similar autosomal DNA and rare recessive traits can create striking physical resemblances. 3. Maternal and paternal matches: The differences in your cousin matches suggest you share different segments of DNA with members of your maternal and paternal lines. DNA is inherited randomly, resulting in variations between siblings. Even though you and your brother share many relatives, you could have inherited matches on only one side from your mother or father. For example, you matched cousin Tommy and Uncle Jim's kids on your paternal side. As first cousins share approximately 25% of their DNA, it's likely that your father's parents are the common ancestors. Your brother may not share this paternal connection, which is why he didn't match with Tommy or Uncle Jim's children. Instead, he inherited DNA segments from his maternal lineage, resulting in unique paternal relatives. 4. Recipe for a test: Considering the genetic variability between siblings and the absence of paternal matches in your brother's results, it might be helpful to clarify relationships with family members. Depending on the company, you may be able to invite your cousins to share their DNA matches and further delineate the maternal and paternal chunks. Concerning the family tree project, I recommend drawing out a storm diagram of maternal and paternal relatives first, then adding matching DNA relatives as blocks. 5. Contacting the DNA company: The discrepancies between your and your brother's results could indicate a misinterpretation of the DNAStructure or downsampling, especially considering the close similarity in your ethnic breakdown. Although rare, DNA testing errors do occur, so you can contact the company's support team about your findings. Suppose the company identifies a problem. In that case, they may request additional samples or suggest upcoming software updates to which you can be entitled, and they might be able to provide a corrected family relationship for your own comparison. It's imperative to remember that DNA only tells part of the story regarding your ancestry and family relationships. To build an accurate and comprehensive family tree, you still require ancestral and descendant documents, oral histories, and phenotypic traits.
